candidate.answerReason: Separate purchases require paying for 6 and 7 windows, respectively. A combined purchase requires paying for 12, saving the price of one window.

methods.label: Group four paid windows with one free window
methods.explanation:
Each offer supplies five windows for the price of four. Since \(7=5+2\), Dave can get one group and two extra windows, paying for \(4+2=6\). Since \(8=5+3\), Doug pays for \(4+3=7\). These are their cheapest separate purchases: paying for one fewer would supply only six and seven windows, respectively.

Together they need \(7+8=15\) windows, exactly three groups of five, so they pay for \(3\cdot4=12\). This is also the cheapest combined purchase: paying for at most eleven windows earns at most two free windows, supplying at most thirteen.

They therefore save
\[
(6+7-12)\cdot100=100
\]
dollars. The answer is \(\boxed{100}\), choice A.
methods.levelReason: Grouping, remainders, and unit-price arithmetic suffice.

candidate.annotationRationale: The mathematical targets are interpreting complete promotional groups and leftover windows, then comparing total prices. Quotient-and-remainder arithmetic supports the grouping method. Percentage discounts and profit equations are not used.

review.mathematicalCheck: Paying for 6 and 7 windows supplies 7 and 8 respectively. Paying one fewer supplies only 6 and 7. Together, paying for 12 supplies 15, whereas at most 11 paid windows supplies at most 13. The saving is $100.
review.levelCheck: Grouping and price arithmetic are elementary, and the minimum-cost comparisons are explicit.
review.methodDistinctness: One complete grouping method is sufficient.
review.annotationCheck: Promotional groups and leftovers fit division-with-remainders applications. Unit price times quantity fits the second target, and quotient-and-remainder computation supports the method.
